questions.question:
Consider the following recurrence relation:

[latex]T(n) = 2T(n-1) + n2^n \quad \text{for} \quad n > 0, \quad T(0) = 1[/latex]

Which ONE of the following options is CORRECT?
questions.explanation:
[latex]T(n)=2T(n-1)+n2^n[/latex]. Substitute [latex]T(n)=2^nS(n)[/latex]:
[latex]2^nS(n)=2\cdot2^{n-1}S(n-1)+n2^n=2^nS(n-1)+n2^n[/latex]
Dividing through by [latex]2^n[/latex]: [latex]S(n)=S(n-1)+n[/latex].

Unrolling this simple recurrence: [latex]S(n)=S(0)+\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}k=1+\dfrac{n(n+1)}{2}=\Theta(n^2)[/latex].

So [latex]T(n)=2^n\cdot\Theta(n^2)=\Theta(n^22^n)[/latex].

Answer: [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n^22^n)[/latex]

Click here for detail solution

questions.question:
Consider an array [latex]A=[10,7,8,19,41,35,25,31][/latex]. Suppose the merge sort algorithm is executed on array [latex]A[/latex] to sort it in increasing order. The merge sort algorithm will carry out a total of [latex]7[/latex] merge operations.

A merge operation on sorted left array [latex]L[/latex] and sorted right array [latex]R[/latex] is said to be void if the output of the merge operation is the elements of array [latex]L[/latex] followed by the elements of array [latex]R[/latex].

The number of void merge operations among these [latex]7[/latex] merge operations is ________. (answer in integer)
questions.explanation:
A merge is void when every element of the left sub-array is already [latex]\le[/latex] every element of the right sub-array, so the merge simply concatenates them with no interleaving.

Trace merge sort on [latex]A=[10,7,8,19,41,35,25,31][/latex]:

Bottom level (pairs):
[latex][10],[7]\to[7,10][/latex] (result is [latex]R[/latex] then [latex]L[/latex], not "[latex]L[/latex] then [latex]R[/latex]") — not void.
[latex][8],[19]\to[8,19][/latex] (already [latex]L[/latex] then [latex]R[/latex] as-is) — void.
[latex][41],[35]\to[35,41][/latex] — not void.
[latex][25],[31]\to[25,31][/latex] (already in order) — void.

Next level (quads):
[latex][7,10]+[8,19]\to[7,8,10,19][/latex] (interleaved, not simply [latex]L[/latex] then [latex]R[/latex]) — not void.
[latex][35,41]+[25,31]\to[25,31,35,41][/latex] (interleaved) — not void.

Final merge:
[latex][7,8,10,19]+[25,31,35,41][/latex]: every element of the left ([latex]\le19[/latex]) is already smaller than every element of the right ([latex]\ge25[/latex]), so the merge is simply [latex]L[/latex] followed by [latex]R[/latex] — void.

Total merges [latex]=4+2+1=7[/latex] (matches the given count), with exactly [latex]3[/latex] of them void.

Answer: 3

questions.question: Which of the following can be recurrence relation(s) corresponding to an algorithm with time complexity [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]?
questions.explanation:
Solve each recurrence and compare to [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex]:

- [latex]T(n)=T(n-1)+1[/latex]: unrolling gives [latex]T(n)=T(1)+(n-1)\times1=\Theta(n)[/latex]. Matches.
- [latex]T(n)=2T(n/2)+1[/latex]: by the Master theorem, [latex]a=2,b=2[/latex] so [latex]n^{\log_2 2}=n^1=n[/latex]; since [latex]f(n)=1[/latex] is polynomially smaller than [latex]n[/latex], Case 1 gives [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n)[/latex]. Matches.
- [latex]T(n)=2T(n/2)+n[/latex]: this is the classic merge-sort recurrence, [latex]f(n)=n=n^{\log_2 2}[/latex] exactly (Case 2), giving [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n\log n)[/latex] — not [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex].
- [latex]T(n)=T(n-1)+n[/latex]: unrolling gives [latex]T(n)=\Theta(1+2+\cdots+n)=\Theta(n^2)[/latex] — not [latex]\Theta(n)[/latex].

Answer: T(n)=T(n-1)+1 and T(n)=2T(n/2)+1 both correspond to Θ(n) algorithms.

questions.question: Let [latex]G(V, E)[/latex] be an undirected and unweighted graph with 100 vertices. Let [latex]d(u, v)[/latex] denote the number of edges in a shortest path between vertices [latex]u[/latex] and [latex]v[/latex] in [latex]V[/latex]. Let the maximum value of [latex]d(u, v)[/latex], [latex]u, v \in V[/latex] such that [latex]u \neq v[/latex], be 30. Let [latex]T[/latex] be any breadth-first-search tree of [latex]G[/latex]. Which ONE of the given options is CORRECT for every such graph [latex]G[/latex]?

options.C: The height of [latex]T[/latex] is at least 15.
options.D: The height of [latex]T[/latex] is at least 30.

questions.explanation:
Let the diameter of the graph be the maximum shortest distance between any two vertices.
It is given that [latex] \max_{u,v\in V,\;u\ne v} d(u,v)=30. [/latex]
Thus, the diameter of the graph is 30.

Relation between BFS Tree Height and Graph Diameter

A Breadth-First Search (BFS) tree rooted at a vertex (r) has the following property:

- The level of every vertex equals its shortest distance from the root.
- Therefore, the height of the BFS tree is the maximum shortest distance from the root to any vertex, which is called the eccentricity of the root.

Let the height of the BFS tree be (h). Then, [latex] h=\max_{v\in V} d(r,v). [/latex]

Using the Diameter

Let the diameter of the graph be (D=30). A well-known property of graphs is [latex] \text{Radius} \ge \left\lceil\frac{D}{2}\right\rceil. [/latex]

Since [latex] D=30, [/latex] we get [latex] \left\lceil\frac{30}{2}\right\rceil=15. [/latex]

Every vertex has eccentricity at least the radius. Hence, regardless of the chosen BFS root, [latex] h\ge 15. [/latex]

The height need not be exactly 15 or exactly 30. It can be any value between 15 and 30 depending on the chosen root.

For example:

- If the BFS starts from a central vertex, the height can be 15.
- If it starts from an end vertex of a diameter, the height can be 30.

Correct Answer: (C) The height of (T) is at least 15.

questions.question: Let [latex]G[/latex] be an undirected connected graph in which every edge has a positive integer weight.  Suppose  that  every  spanning  tree  in  [latex]G[/latex]  has  even  weight.  Which  of  the following statements is/are TRUE for every such graph [latex]G[/latex] ?

options.A: All edges in [latex]G[/latex] have even weight
options.B: All edges in [latex]G[/latex] have even weight OR all edges in [latex]G[/latex] have odd weight
options.C: In each cycle [latex]G[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex], all edges in [latex]G[/latex] have even weight
options.D: In each cycle [latex]G[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex], either all edges in [latex]G[/latex] have even weight OR all edges in [latex]G[/latex] have odd weight

questions.explanation:
Take any cycle C and two edges [latex]e,f[/latex] on it. Extend the path [latex]C-f[/latex] to a spanning tree T (it contains [latex]e[/latex], not [latex]f[/latex]). Then [latex]T'=T-e+f[/latex] is also a spanning tree.

[latex]w(T')-w(T)=w(f)-w(e)[/latex]. Both trees are even, so [latex]w(f)-w(e)[/latex] is even [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]e[/latex] and [latex]f[/latex] have the same parity. So in every cycle all edges are even or all are odd [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Counter-examples for the rest:
- Triangle with all weights 1: every spanning tree has weight 2 (even), yet edges are odd [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] options 1 and 3 FALSE.
- Path with weights 1, 1, 2: only spanning tree has weight 4, but edges are mixed [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] option 2 FALSE.

Answer: In each cycle, either all edges have even weight OR all edges have odd weight

questions.question:
Consider a table [latex]T[/latex], where the elements [latex]T[i][j], 0 \leq i, j \leq n[/latex], represent the cost of the optimal solutions of different subproblems of a problem that is being solved using a dynamic programming algorithm. The recursive formulation to compute the table entries is as follows:

[latex] \begin{array}{ll} T[0][k]=T[k][0]=1 & \text { for } k=0,1,2, \ldots, n \\ T[i][j]=2 T[i-1][j]+3 T[i][j-1] & \text { for } 1 \leq i, j \leq n \end{array} [/latex]

Consider the following two algorithms to compute entries of [latex]T[/latex]. Assume that for both the algorithms, for all [latex]0 \leq i, j \leq n, T[i][j][/latex] has been initialized to [latex]1[/latex].

[latex]\begin{aligned} &\text{Algorithm } B_1: \\ &\quad \text{For } i = 1,2,\ldots,n \\ &\quad\quad \text{For } j = 1,2,\ldots,n \\ &\quad\quad\quad T[i][j] = 2T[i-1][j] + 3T[i][j-1] \\[6pt] &\text{Algorithm } B_2: \\ &\quad \text{For } s = 2,3,\ldots,2n \\ &\quad\quad \text{For } i = 1,2,\ldots,n \\ &\quad\quad\quad \text{For } j = 1,2,\ldots,n \\ &\quad\quad\quad\quad \text{If } i + j = = s \\ &\quad\quad\quad\quad\quad T[i][j] = 2T[i-1][j] + 3T[i][j-1] \end{aligned}[/latex]

Algorithm [latex]B_{k}, k \in\{1,2\}[/latex] is said to be correct if and only if it calculates the correct values of [latex]T[i][j][/latex], for all [latex]0 \leq i, j \leq n[/latex], (as per the recursive formulation) at the end of the execution of the algorithm [latex]B_{k}[/latex].

Which one of the following statements is true?

options.B: Algorithm [latex]B_{1}[/latex] is correct, but algorithm [latex]B_{2}[/latex] is incorrect
options.C: Algorithm [latex]B_{2}[/latex] is correct, but algorithm [latex]B_{1}[/latex] is incorrect

questions.explanation:
To correctly compute [latex]T[i][j]=2T[i-1][j]+3T[i][j-1][/latex], both dependencies — [latex]T[i-1][j][/latex] (the cell directly above) and [latex]T[i][j-1][/latex] (the cell directly to the left) — must already hold their final, correct values before [latex]T[i][j][/latex] is computed.

Algorithm B1 (row-major: outer loop over [latex]i[/latex], inner over [latex]j[/latex]): when computing [latex]T[i][j][/latex], [latex]T[i-1][j][/latex] was already finalized in the previous (fully completed) [latex]i-1[/latex] row, and [latex]T[i][j-1][/latex] was already finalized earlier in the same row (since [latex]j-1Correct.

Algorithm B2 (processes cells in order of increasing anti-diagonal [latex]s=i+j[/latex]): for a cell [latex]T[i][j][/latex] with [latex]i+j=s[/latex], its dependency [latex]T[i-1][j][/latex] lies on diagonal [latex]s-1[/latex] and [latex]T[i][j-1][/latex] also lies on diagonal [latex]s-1[/latex] — both are processed in the strictly earlier iteration [latex]s-1Correct.

Answer: Both algorithms B1 and B2 are correct.

questions.question:
Consider the decision problem 2CNFSAT defined as follows:
{ [latex]\phi[/latex] | [latex]\phi[/latex] is a satisfiable propositional formula in CNF with at most two literal per clause}
For example, [latex]\phi =(x_{1} \vee x_{2}) \wedge (x_{1} \vee \bar{x_{3}}) \wedge (x_{2} \vee x_{4})[/latex] is a Boolean formula and it is in 2CNFSAT.
The decision problem 2CNFSAT is

options.B: solvable in polynomial time by reduction to directed graph reachability.
options.C: solvable in constant time since any input instance is satisfiable

questions.explanation:
Each clause [latex](a\vee b)[/latex] gives implications [latex] eg a ightarrow b[/latex] and [latex] eg b ightarrow a[/latex]. The formula is unsatisfiable iff some x reaches [latex] eg x[/latex] and [latex] eg x[/latex] reaches x in this implication graph.

So 2-SAT is solved in polynomial (linear) time by graph reachability.

Answer: solvable in polynomial time by reduction to directed graph reachability

Let [latex]U = \{1, 2, 3\}[/latex]. Let [latex]2^U[/latex] denote the powerset of [latex]U[/latex]. Consider an undirected graph [latex]G[/latex] whose vertex set is [latex]2^U[/latex]. For any [latex]A,B \in 2^U, (A,B)[/latex] is an edge in [latex]G[/latex] if and only if (i) [latex]A \neq B[/latex], and (ii) either [latex]A \subseteq B[/latex] or [latex]B \subseteq A[/latex]. For any vertex [latex]A[/latex] in [latex]G[/latex], the set of all possible orderings in which the vertices of [latex]G[/latex] can be visited in a Breadth First Search (BFS) starting from [latex]A[/latex] is denoted by [latex]B(A)[/latex].
If [latex]\phi [/latex] denotes the empty set, then the cardinality of [latex]B(\phi ) [/latex] is ____.
questions.explanation:
[latex]\phi[/latex] is a subset of every set, so [latex]\phi[/latex] is adjacent to all the other [latex]2^3-1=7[/latex] vertices.

BFS from [latex]\phi[/latex] visits all 7 neighbours at level 1, and these 7 can be visited in any order: [latex]7!=5040[/latex].

Answer: 5040

questions.question:
Consider the following recurrence relation:
[latex] T(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{c} \sqrt{n} T(\sqrt{n})+n \text { for } n \geq 1, \\ 1 \quad \text { for } n=1 . \end{array}\right. [/latex]
Which one of the following options is CORRECT?
questions.explanation:
Divide both sides by [latex]n[/latex]: [latex]\frac{T(n)}{n}=\frac{T(\sqrt n)}{\sqrt n}+1[/latex].

Let [latex]S(n)=\frac{T(n)}{n}[/latex]. Then [latex]S(n)=S(\sqrt n)+1[/latex].

Taking square roots repeatedly, [latex]n\to n^{1/2}\to n^{1/4}\to\cdots[/latex] reaches a constant after [latex]\log\log n[/latex] steps, adding 1 each step. So [latex]S(n)=\Theta(\log\log n)[/latex].

[latex]T(n)=n\,S(n)=\Theta(n\log\log n)[/latex]

Answer: [latex]T(n)=\Theta(n\log\log n)[/latex]

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow

- 1-3-4-2: 4 + 2 + 3 = 9, 1-0-3-2: 9

Answer: 8
